newsitem.title: PERU: Peru wants investment, not cash for La Oroya.
newsitem.headline: Peru wants investment, not cash for La Oroya.

text.p: The upcoming auction of the Peruvian government's largest mining asset is likely to help the huge La Oroya metallurgic complex fulfill its potential after decades of poor performance, according to analysts.

State miner Centromin has designed the terms of the April 14 sale to achieve maximum investment in the outdated complex of refineries and smelters after years of insufficient investment, Morgan Grenfell head of research in Lima Guillermo Arbe said.

Earlier this week, Centromin set a $70 million minimum bid price for the auction, whose terms oblige the winning firm to immediately inject the money offered at the sale into the complex as capital and then invest a further $120 million over the next five years.

Unlike previous mining privatizations, the state treasury will receive no cash from the sale of La Oroya, which lies in the country's central Andes 12,300 feet (3,700 meters) above sea level and 120 miles (190 km) east of Lima.
"It makes sense," Arbe said. "You have an asset that is not being used efficiently, so your priority is (realizing) the asset's potential -- not putting money in treasury."

Alicia Campos, mining analyst at local brokerage Provalor, also welcomed Centromin's emphasis on attracting new investment for the complex, whose previous two sale attempts failed due to the severe environmental liabilities of an asset first built in 1921.
"The most important thing here is the investment commitment," Campos said.

"Once the winner has invested the money, the modern technology will make the asset more valuable for the company and provide Peru with a large complex functioning without problems after years of operating without the appropriate environmental conditions."
La Oroya, which now processes 22 metals and their byproducts, is Centromin's largest asset and the biggest test for its piecemeal privatization, the analysts said.

But after last year's series of Centromin sales attracted the world's largest mining companies to pay hundreds of millions of dollars and make investment commitments worth billions, the state miner appears to have also found the right formula for La Oroya.
"There are various firms interested," Josilu Carbonel, mining analyst at Santander Investment in Lima, said.

For months Mexico's Industrias Penoles S.A. has been touted by industry sources as the firm most keen to buy the complex but last month Centromin said the Doe Run Co of the United States had also shown "strong interest" in the sale.

The idea of state coffers receiving no immediate income from the sale could have created a political storm a year ago when Peru's privatization drive met with rowdy opposition. But last year's lucrative sales have quieted resistance.
"There would have been arguments had this been the first (sale). But given the circumstances there should be no problems," Arbe said.
In part, the public has swung round in favor of privatizations because the government has shown it can be tough on buyers who do not comply with their investment commitments.

Last month, Centromin bared its teeth when it announced Brazil's Paranapanema had lost its option to buy polymetallic mine Yauliyacu claiming the firm did not provide the necessary paperwork and guarantee.
"The government wants to show that it is firm when it comes to investment commitments," Carbonel said.
